entries.definition: A directed latent sequence-model family in which several independently evolving hidden Markov chains jointly determine the observation distribution at each time.
entries.identity_notes: This record covers the independent-chain factorial HMM developed by Ghahramani and Jordan, with a shared observation distribution. It is not a mixture selecting one HMM, a globally normalized product of complete HMM likelihoods, an input-conditioned HMM, or the variational algorithm used to fit the model. Each combination of chain states is one joint state; factorial refers to its distributed component representation. The later coupled-chain and input-conditioned extensions in Section 5 are outside this narrow definition. limitations: Independent latent dynamics do not imply posterior independence after shared observations. Special emission structures may decouple chains; for the Gaussian case a sufficient condition is cross-chain orthogonality in the C^-1 metric. Note 3’s ordinary orthogonality with a merely diagonal covariance is not sufficient in general.

The Gaussian additive mean is a worked parameterization, not the only possible factorial-HMM emission. Its closed-form parameter updates do not automatically transfer to nonlinear or discrete emissions.

Factorized transitions reduce exact computation relative to a naive unconstrained joint-state HMM but do not remove exponential state growth. A compact parameterization is not a universal scalability or accuracy guarantee.

Approximate E-steps may improve a variational bound without monotonically improving the true likelihood. Additive offsets are not individually identifiable without conventions; the paper uses a pseudoinverse.

claims.statement: With independent initial states and chain-specific transitions, the joint distribution factors into the product of chain priors, the product over times and chains of p(s_t^m|s_(t-1)^m), and one shared p(y_t|s_t^1,...,s_t^M) per time. The paper’s worked emission is Gaussian with mean sum_m W_m s_t^m for one-hot states and common covariance C. Although chains are independent a priori, observations generally couple their posterior paths through the shared emission. For M chains each having K states, the joint latent state has K^M configurations. Exact forward–backward can exploit the transition factorization by contracting one chain dimension at a time, with O(T M K^(M+1)) transition work under the paper’s fixed-observation-dimension setting; this remains exponential in M. EM uses posterior state, temporal-pair and cross-chain moments. In the additive Gaussian model its weight update is a linear-system solution with a pseudoinverse because chain contributions have redundant mean offsets. Exact inference, Gibbs sampling and variational approximations are separate procedures, not defining alternatives for model identity.

entries.name: Input-output hidden Markov model
entries.definition: A conditional latent sequence-model family whose discrete hidden-state transitions and state-specific observation distributions depend on the current external input.
entries.identity_notes: The inspected Bengio–Frasconi model maps an input sequence to an output-sequence distribution using a latent Markov state. Its original modular neural implementation supplies input-sensitive transition and output subnetworks, but the model family is identified by the conditional factorization. It differs from a standard autonomous HMM, a factorial multi-chain model, an undirected product of HMMs, a generic recurrent network and an arithmetic mixture without state dynamics. The input sequence is conditioned on rather than assigned its own generative model. limitations: Input-conditioned transitions can vary with time even with fixed parameters. Removing input dependence recovers an ordinary HMM special case; no claim is made that an arbitrary recurrent network has this normalized latent-state model.

The recurrent probability vector is a distribution over states, not a single sampled state path. Output-conditioned filtering or smoothing must include observed output likelihoods; the input-only recurrence is insufficient for that posterior.

The paper’s backward variable includes the current emission, unlike a common future-only convention. Its pair-posterior Equation (11) must be interpreted with that convention to avoid counting the emission twice.

The special lookup-table re-estimation display in Equation (12) omits an old transition factor needed by the posterior-count expression in Equation (11). This record uses posterior-weighted EM/GEM semantics and does not certify that display as a general update formula.

GEM inherits conditional-likelihood monotonicity when its expected objective is increased with an exact E-step; an arbitrary gradient step, global optimum or unconditional convergence to a local maximum is not guaranteed. Local optima and large state spaces are practical limitations acknowledged by the source.

The grammar experiment reports accuracy conditional on successful training runs and selects model size using validation strings. No universal long-memory advantage, benchmark ranking, 1996 full-text claim or author-code behavior is curated.

claims.statement: Given inputs u_1:T and an initial state distribution, sum over paths in p(s_0) times product_t p(s_t|s_(t-1),u_t) p(y_t|s_t,u_t) to obtain p(y_1:T|u_1:T). The original architecture uses one static transition subnetwork per previous state, with a softmax over allowed successors, and one output subnetwork per current state. Recursively propagating zeta_t(i)=sum_j p(s_t=i|s_(t-1)=j,u_t) zeta_(t-1)(j) gives the state distribution conditional on inputs alone; it is distinct from the posterior after conditioning on observed target outputs. Forward–backward with the observed output factors supplies state and transition posterior responsibilities for conditional-likelihood EM. The expected complete-data log likelihood separates into responsibility-weighted log transition and log emission terms. Neural parameterizations can use generalized EM updates that increase that expected objective. Intermittently missing outputs can be marginalized by replacing their normalized emission factors by one while preserving the latent chain.

entries.definition: A variational inference procedure for factorial hidden Markov models that approximates the posterior by independent chain-path distributions while retaining temporal dependence within each chain.
entries.identity_notes: This record denotes the chain-structured approximation and additive-Gaussian updates in Ghahramani–Jordan Section 3.5 and Appendix D. It is narrower than all structured variational inference and distinct from the factorial HMM model, a fully factorized state-by-time approximation, exact joint-state forward–backward, Gibbs sampling, or BBVI score-function optimization. It requires neither an amortized recognition network nor a variational autoencoder architecture. limitations: The approximation removes posterior dependence between chains even when the shared observation creates explaining-away effects. It preserves each chain’s time dependence, unlike a fully factorized state-by-time distribution.

The h factors are positive unnormalized potentials, not row-normalized transition probabilities or already-normalized state posteriors. Normalization and initial/boundary conditions belong to the complete chain computation.

The residual/diagonal formula depends on additive Gaussian emissions with common covariance. General emissions require their own expected-log-factor calculations; the formula is not an arbitrary-model black-box update.

Coordinate-ascent guarantees require an exact update of one factor while holding the others fixed. Simultaneous arbitrary updates, local stopping criteria or approximate model steps do not establish a global optimum, exact evidence, or universal likelihood improvement.

Appendix C Equation C.9 displays prior/transition signs inconsistent with its energy definition and derivative; that display is not adopted. Appendix D cancels explicit prior/transition log terms when the same factors are retained, but its moments and normalizer still depend on those factors; the accompanying independence wording is not literal total independence.

The general product-of-path-distributions variational family contains independent-time factors, but the displayed fixed-transition/unary parameterization and local optimization do not justify claiming every run outperforms a fully factorized approximation. No benchmark or author implementation is certified.

claims.statement: For fixed model parameters and observations, choose q(S)=product_m q_m(s_1:T^m) and optimize the evidence lower bound E_q[log p(Y,S)-log q(S)], equivalently minimizing KL(q||p(S|Y)). Each chain factor is globally normalized over its path and retains the model’s initial and transition factors multiplied by positive unary potentials h_t^m. In the additive Gaussian model, h_t^m is proportional to exp((W_m)^T C^-1 [y_t-sum_(l!=m) W_l E_q[s_t^l]] - 0.5 diag((W_m)^T C^-1 W_m)), componentwise over the chain’s states. With other chain factors fixed, run forward–backward using these unary factors to update that chain’s state and temporal-pair moments, then repeat across chains. Same-time moments between different chains factorize under q; within-chain temporal moments do not. Such exact single-chain coordinate updates increase or preserve the bound for fixed model parameters. The moments may also supply a variational E-step for model fitting, but this approximate posterior does not become the exact posterior merely by convergence.

Separate forward–backward computations evaluate the unnormalized product and complete-data hidden posteriors; they do not by themselves give the product’s global normalizer or exact likelihood. Small finite models can be enumerated, but this does not establish scalable tractability.

When observations are missing or future observations are integrated out, the experts can become dependent. Exact separate posterior inference given a complete sequence is not a claim of equally simple causal prediction from a prefix.

CD learning is approximate, and the customary short-chain update is not generally an exact likelihood or contrastive-objective gradient. The Brown paper’s initial pseudocode writes probability derivatives where its final update uses log derivatives; this record follows the log-score update supported by the later explicit formulation.

native_neighbors.definition: A variational-inference procedure that estimates evidence-lower-bound gradients from samples of a tractable variational distribution using its score function and model log joint, with mean-field local signals and score control variates to manage estimator variance.
native_neighbors.identity_notes: This record covers Ranganath, Gerrish and Blei’s original BBVI Algorithms 1–2 and their score-function estimator, mean-field local signals and control variates. It is not every black-box inference method, a pathwise reparameterization estimator, a model architecture or an amortized recognition network such as NVIL. The hierarchical data-subsampling extension is outside the validated mechanism scope here. No normalized identity match was found across all 442 pinned AIO labels/scoped synonyms and 337 preceding native IDs/names/aliases. limitations: Black box still requires sampling from and evaluating the variational distribution, score derivatives with respect to its parameters, and evaluation of the model log joint at sampled latent states. The method does not require differentiation through a discrete latent sample, but support and integrability conditions remain necessary.

Raw unbiasedness requires the regularity assumptions behind differentiation under the expectation and zero expected score. A model normalization constant independent of lambda cancels from this gradient; a parameter-dependent term cannot be discarded on that basis.

A coefficient fixed independently of the gradient samples preserves expectation when the relevant moments exist. A coefficient estimated from those same samples can correlate with the sample score and introduce bias. The paper reports separate sample counts for coefficient estimation and gradient calculation, but the inspected description does not establish an exact sampling-independence convention; no implementation behavior is asserted.

Population-optimal control-variate scaling and conditional-expectation variance reduction do not guarantee that estimated coefficients or every additional removal of zero-mean terms reduces finite-sample variance. Zero or poorly estimated score variance requires handling beyond division by the displayed ratio.

The practical step schedule and change-in-parameters stopping rule do not establish global optimality or exact posterior recovery. Mean-field factorization can limit the approximation. The printed hierarchical subsampling formulas need a separate weighting audit and are not curated as a verified extension here.
No benchmark result, author-code run, general convergence proof or posterior-quality certification is included.

claims.statement: For fixed observed x and joint model p(x,z), choose a variational family q(z;lambda), sample z from q, and maximize L(lambda)=E_q[log p(x,z)-log q(z;lambda)] by stochastic ascent. Under the normalized-score and differentiation-under-expectation conditions, the raw gradient is E_q[grad_lambda log q(z;lambda)*(log p(x,z)-log q(z;lambda))], estimated by a Monte Carlo average. The mean-field version factors q into q_i(z_i;lambda_i) and uses for each factor the model log terms that depend on z_i together with -log q_i; unrelated terms cancel in expectation under the stated factorization. For parameter coordinate d in factor i, let h_d be the score and f_d be that score times the local log signal. A fixed control-variate coefficient gives f_d-a_d*h_d because E[h_d]=0; the population variance-minimizing coefficient is Cov(f_d,h_d)/Var(h_d) when these quantities exist and Var(h_d)>0. The source estimates coefficients from samples and averages corrected contributions before a stochastic-ascent update. Its fixed-coefficient expectation identity does not by itself justify arbitrary reuse of samples to estimate both the coefficient and corrected gradient.
